title: Cartloads of books
hook: read cartloads of books, but only one thing counts; all else is ego's talk (Asa di Var, ang 467)

segments.voice: Yesterday, haumai: ego is an illness, and its cure is within. Today, one of the places ego hides best: in what we know.

A list of books to read someday. Podcasts saved for later. Tabs opened and never closed. It's a strange modern condition: drowning in things to know, and still unsure of the main thing. Guru Nanak lived when a book was copied by hand, a precious object. And still he pictured someone with so many books they had to be hauled away in carts. Then he asked what all of it was worth.
screen: `A LIST OF BOOKS TO READ.` → `DROWNING IN THINGS TO KNOW.` → `BOOKS HAULED AWAY IN CARTS.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 467, and its pictures pile up on purpose. In paraphrase: you could read and read and fill whole carts with books. You could read and load caravans. You could read and fill boats, and fill pits. You could read for years and years, every month of the year, your whole life, with every breath. And then the last line drops like a stone. Nanak, only one thing is counted. Ik gal. Everything else is ego's babble. Gal is everyday Punjabi for a thing, a matter, a word said. Only one matter goes into the account. What is it? The salok doesn't spell it out in that line, but Sikh teachers read it as the Name, remembering the One, lived in the heart. And notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say. He doesn't say reading is bad. The Gurus were poets and scholars. Sikh tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping the Gurmukhi script and teaching people to read it. Gurdwaras read from the Guru Granth Sahib every day. The point is what reading is for. Learning that only makes a bigger pile, a bigger I who knows more, is yesterday's ego in a new outfit. Learning that leads to one thing, lived, is something else. The very next salok says it sharply: the more one writes and reads, the more one burns. Set beside this salok, the burning is learning that only feeds the self. There's relief in this. You don't have to get through the whole pile. You only have to let one line actually change you.
screen: `CARTS, CARAVANS, BOATS OF BOOKS.` · `ONLY ONE THING IS COUNTED.` · `READING ISN'T THE PROBLEM.` · `LET ONE LINE CHANGE YOU.` · then, large: `ONE THING COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Choose one line you've met on this path, maybe today's, only one thing is counted, and say it slowly, once. Say it again and stop on each word; notice which one catches, and if your mind rushes on, come back to the one line. If you pray, say Waheguru between the repetitions.
Ik gal, one thing, one matter: Guru Nanak's picture of endless reading, carts, caravans and boats of it, says only ik gal is counted; the rest is ego's talk.
Your line: one thing counts. You don't have to finish the pile. Day five hundred forty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing Gurbani daily, and this salok of Asa di Var, sung at dawn, reminds them that reading is meant to lead to remembering the One, not to a pile of knowledge.

original.note: Gurmukhi: one thing, one matter; gal is everyday Punjabi for a thing said or a matter.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guru Nanak didn't like books.
what it means: reading only counts when it leads to the one thing, the Name, lived; otherwise it feeds the ego.
what a scholar hears: the salok stacks measures of reading, carts, caravans, years, breaths, then ends 'lekhai ik gal': in the account, one thing.

chat.says: So does Guru Nanak think reading lots of books is bad?
options: No, the point is what reading is for: one thing, lived, not a bigger pile.
Yes, he says books are ego's babble, so a Sikh should mostly stop reading.
No, he says the more you read, the more is counted in your favor at the end.
chat.meaning: The Gurus were poets and scholars. The salok says only ik gal is counted; learning that only feeds the self is ego's talk.

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm the measures (carts, caravans/saath, boats, pits, years, months, a lifetime, every breath) and the closing 'Nanak lekhai ik gal hor haumai jhakhnaa jhaakh'.
Reading 'ik gal' as the Name is given as how Sikh teachers read it; confirm.
Guru Angad and the Gurmukhi script: phrased as 'remembered for shaping... and encouraging'; confirm wording, since historians differ on how far he devised the script.
The next salok ('likh likh parhiaa tetaa karhiaa') is paraphrased as 'the more one writes and reads, the more one burns'; confirm the reading.
